newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary publishes draft tender for TV channels.
newsitem.headline: Hungary publishes draft tender for TV channels.

text.p: Hungary on Thursday published the draft tender for ten-year concessions for two national television channels in a bid to privatise a large part of its state-dominated television market by May 1997.
The potentially lucrative channels, the state-owned MTV2 and another planned commercial channel, are expected to attract several large foreign investors.
"We have pubished the text -- alea iacta est, the die has been cast," Mihaly T. Revesz, head of the National Radio and Television Authority (ORTT) told a news conference.
He added that the ORTT will publish the final text of the tenders by December 23, following a last consultation with the potential investors on December 11.

The bids should be submitted by March, and the ORTT will select those which will take part in the second round of the tenders in the middle of April. The contracts are expected to be concluded at the end of May.

The ORTT will rank the bidders on a 100-point scale, on which the offered concession fee would be worth a maximum 40 points, the programme plan up to 35 points and the business plan a maximum 10 points.

Revesz said the minimum concession fee of eight billion forints for ten years, which the ORTT planned to require from bidders, was low and was likely to increase as a result of fierce competition among bidders.
"We experienced large international interest (in the concessions)," he added.
Several years of political discussion about media law have left Hungary well behind most other central European countries in the privatisation of media companies.
The law, which aims at liberalising the media market by opening up national radio and television channels for investors, was finally passed early this year.
Revesz said Hungary expected to create a dual television market of state-owned and private channels, with the two private channels launching services from September 1 next year.
"We plan to have three national public service channels and two national commercial channels on the menu for television viewers by September 1," he said.
Analysts said earlier that the main attraction for investors was advertising revenue.

In 1995, official TV advertising expenditure in Hungary was 26 billion forints, but the actual amount spent on publicity, taking into account sponsorship and advertising disguised as arts patronage, could be 20 percent higher, analysts said.
Compagnie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT) group, which recently merged with Germany's Bertelsmann, is one international media company to express interest.

Press reports said earlier that potential bidders also included the Central European Development Corporation, led by former U.S. ambassador to Hungary Mark Palmer, the German Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung group and France's TF1.
